intro:
The best leaf vacuum for most yards is the WORX WG509 TriVac, a corded 3-in-1 that WORX rates at an 18:1 mulch ratio feeding a 1.2-bushel bag. That combination means fewer trips to the bin than any other handheld here.

Below are seven picks: four corded blower/vac/mulchers, two battery models and one push sweeper for open lawns. Each one is ranked on the two numbers that decide how a leaf vacuum feels in October, how finely it shreds and how much it holds, followed by the questions buyers ask most about cords, wet leaves and impellers.
quickAnswer: Buy the WORX WG509 TriVac for a typical suburban lot: 18:1 rated mulching, a metal impeller, a 1.2-bushel bag and a 3-year warranty. Pick the Toro UltraPlus 51621 for the strongest vacuum-mode airflow (405 CFM), the Sun Joe SBJ606E for the biggest handheld bag, or the Ryobi RY40451 if you want a cordless vacuum that shreds at 16:1.

Airspeed in MPH matters less on a leaf vacuum than on a blower. The vacuum only has to lift what sits under the tube, so mulch ratio, bag capacity, impeller material and the weight hanging off your shoulder decide whether the job takes one hour or three.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Leaf Vacuums in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
Every number below comes from the maker's product page, spec sheet or manual. Where a brand does not publish a figure, such as bag size, it is left blank rather than estimated. Owner feedback is summarized as patterns, not quotes.

### Best Overall: WORX WG509 TriVac

The WG509 earns the top spot because it leads the handheld field on the spec that saves the most walking. WORX rates it at an 18:1 mulch ratio, produced by a two-stage metal impeller with a shredder blade behind it, and it empties into a 1.2-bushel shoulder bag (about 11 gallons). Switching from blowing to vacuuming takes a lever flip rather than a tube swap, and electronic variable speed lets you ease off near mulch beds.

The spec sheet lists a 12-amp motor, 350 CFM, up to 210 MPH and a weight of 9.3 pounds, and WORX backs it with a 3-year warranty, the longest of the corded picks. The catches are the usual corded ones: you have to manage an extension cord, and on a lot with several mature oaks the 1.2-bushel bag still fills often. For a quarter-acre yard with beds and a driveway, it does the most shredding per trip.

**Pros:** highest rated mulch ratio among the handhelds; metal two-stage impeller plus blade; lever mode switch; 3-year warranty.

**Cons:** cord limits reach; bag fills quickly on heavily wooded lots.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=WORX+WG509+TriVac&tag=sktiger-20)

### Most Vacuum Airflow: Toro UltraPlus 51621

If suction is what you care about, the UltraPlus is the pick. Toro lists 405 CFM in vacuum mode and 340 CFM blowing, with air speed up to 260 MPH, the highest vacuum-mode figure published for any model here. Metal impeller blades and Toro's Shredz-All ring handle the mulching, which Toro describes as up to 97% leaf reduction rather than as a ratio, noting that results depend on the material.

An infinitely variable speed dial lets you turn the blower down to a whisper near flower beds. The cost is weight: at 13 pounds it is the heaviest handheld on the list, and Toro does not publish bag capacity. The warranty is 2 years, and Toro's dealer network makes parts easier to find than with some budget brands. Choose it when leaves pile deep and pull matters more than a light tool.

**Pros:** 405 CFM rated vacuum airflow; metal impeller and shred ring; variable speed; dealer and parts network.

**Cons:** 13 lb; no published bag size or mulch ratio.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Toro+UltraPlus+51621&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Value, Biggest Bag: Sun Joe SBJ606E

The SBJ606E puts the most motor and the biggest bag of any corded handheld here into one tool. Sun Joe lists a 14-amp motor, 440 CFM in vacuum mode, blowing speeds up to 250 MPH and a 16:1 mulch ratio through an aluminum alloy impeller. The 18-gallon bag works out to nearly 2 bushels, roughly half again what the WORX holds, and the listed net weight is 9.1 pounds.

Sun Joe calls it a 4-in-1 because a gutter-cleaning attachment joins the blow, vacuum and mulch modes. You give up two points of mulch ratio against the WG509 and get a 2-year warranty instead of three, and a big bag gets heavy once it is full. If your priority is fewer stops to empty, this is the corded pick to buy.

**Pros:** 18-gallon bag; 14 A motor and 440 CFM rated vacuum airflow; aluminum alloy impeller; gutter kit included.

**Cons:** 16:1 trails the WORX; 2-year warranty; full bag is heavy.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Sun+Joe+SBJ606E&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Basic Corded: BLACK+DECKER BV6600

The BV6600 is the blower/vac you can usually find on a store shelf the same afternoon. BLACK+DECKER lists a 12-amp motor, blowing speed up to 250 MPH and a 16-to-1 reduction claim, with a high-impact metal fan the brand says resists clogging. It ships with a blower tube, a vacuum tube and a concentrator nozzle for prying leaves out of corners, plus a reusable shoulder bag with a quick-empty zipper; the manual also lists a disposable-bag option for big cleanups.

What holds it back is missing data. BLACK+DECKER does not publish CFM or bag capacity, and its weight figures vary between listings, so it is hard to compare head to head. The warranty is 2 years. Buy it when the WORX and Sun Joe are out of stock and you need a proven 16:1 vac today.

**Pros:** 16:1 rated reduction; metal fan; reusable and disposable bag options; widely stocked.

**Cons:** no published CFM or bag size; weight unclear; 2-year warranty.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=BLACK%2BDECKER+BV6600&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Cordless 3-in-1: WORX WG583 40V Power Share

The WG583 is the cordless blower/vac/mulcher for spots far from an outlet. It runs on two 20V Power Share batteries for 40 volts with a brushless motor, and the kit WORX lists includes two 4.0Ah batteries and a dual charger. The spec table gives 350 CFM and 185 MPH on high, a 12:1 mulch ratio through a two-stage impeller and a 1.0-bushel bag.

It is the lightest powered pick here, 5.5 pounds bare and 8.4 pounds with batteries installed. The trade-offs follow from the battery: a lower mulch ratio, a smaller bag and runtime you have to plan around. WORX does not name the impeller material. It shines on patios, beds, decks and garages, and the bare-tool version is an inexpensive add if you already own WORX 20V packs.

**Pros:** no cord, brushless; 8.4 lb with batteries; shares batteries with WORX 20V tools; kit includes two batteries.

**Cons:** 12:1 mulch ratio; 1.0-bushel bag; impeller material not stated.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=WORX+WG583+blower+vac+mulcher&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Cordless Vacuum-Only: Ryobi 40V RY40451

Ryobi's 40V leaf vacuum drops the blower and puts everything into pickup and shredding. Ryobi rates it at 16:1 through a metal impeller, matching the better corded handhelds and well ahead of the cordless WORX. Small adjustable wheels carry the intake along the ground, so you roll it across a patio or along a bed edge instead of holding a tube at arm's length.

Ryobi quotes more than 30 minutes of runtime on a 40V 4Ah battery. The tool weighs 12.7 pounds, which the wheels help offset, and Ryobi covers it with a 5-year limited warranty, the longest here. Ryobi does not publish bag capacity or airflow. There is no blower mode, and the wheels prefer hard surfaces and short grass to rough ground. If you already run Ryobi 40V tools, start here.

**Pros:** 16:1 mulch with a metal impeller; wheels carry the weight; 30+ minutes on a 4Ah pack; 5-year warranty.

**Cons:** no blower mode; 12.7 lb; bag capacity not published.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ryobi+40V+leaf+vacuum+mulcher+RY40451&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Open Lawns: Agri-Fab 45-0218 Push Sweeper

The Agri-Fab 45-0218 is not a vacuum at all, which is exactly why it belongs here. On a lawn that is mostly open grass, a push sweeper picks up leaves faster and more quietly than any handheld. Brushes geared to the wheels at a 5.0:1 ratio sweep a 26-inch path into a hopper rated at 6.2 cubic feet, about 46 gallons, or roughly four times a typical handheld bag.

It rolls on 9.8-inch wheels and Agri-Fab lists it at 26 pounds, with no motor, fuel, cord, battery or noise. The limits are just as clear: it does not mulch, it struggles with wet or matted leaves, and it cannot reach into beds or along fence lines. Many owners pair one with a corded vacuum for the edges.

**Pros:** 6.2 cu ft hopper; no fuel, cord, battery or noise; 26-inch path.

**Cons:** no mulching; poor on wet leaves; cannot reach beds and corners.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Agri-Fab+45-0218+lawn+sweeper&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: What Is the Difference Between a Leaf Vacuum, a Blower and a Mulcher?
sections.body:
A blower pushes leaves, a vacuum pulls them up a tube, and a mulcher chops them on the way into the bag so the bag holds more. Nearly every handheld sold as a leaf vacuum today is all three in one body: the same motor and impeller either push air out a narrow blower tube or draw it in through a wider vacuum tube.

### How mulching happens inside the tool

In vacuum mode, leaves race up the tube and hit the spinning impeller before they reach the bag. That collision is the mulching. Tools with a second stage, like the shredder blade behind the WG509 impeller or the shred ring in the Toro, cut the fragments again so they pack more tightly. The bag hangs from a shoulder strap and you unzip it into a yard-waste bag or compost bin when it fills.

### Where each mode earns its keep

Use blower mode to clear the driveway, chase leaves out of a bed or herd them into a pile. Switch to vacuum mode for the pile itself and for the places a rake handles badly: along fences, in window wells, behind shrubs and in corners where a blower only stirs things up.

Trying to vacuum an entire open lawn is where most owners give up. The intake is only a few inches wide and the bag fills in minutes. Open turf is better handled by blowing into windrows, a push sweeper, or a mulching mower; our [self-propelled lawn mower guide](/best-self-propelled-lawn-mower/) covers the mowers that mulch leaves well.

sections.heading: What Does the Mulch Ratio on a Leaf Vacuum Mean?
sections.body:
A mulch ratio is the maker's claim for how many bags of loose, whole leaves shrink into one bag after shredding. At 16:1, sixteen bags of dry leaves should become one bag of mulch. Compared with 16:1, a 12:1 tool fills about a third more bags for the same yard, and an 18:1 tool fills about 11% fewer.

### Treat the number as relative

Makers rate mulch ratios with dry leaves in good conditions, and each brand uses its own method. Owners commonly report that real reduction falls short of the box once leaves are damp or mixed with twigs and pine needles. What the ratio does tell you is how aggressive the shredding system is. The 18:1 WG509 adds a blade behind its impeller; the 12:1 rating on the compact cordless WORX reflects a smaller motor and housing.

### Percentages are not ratios

Toro states up to 97% reduction for the UltraPlus instead of a ratio. On paper that would be better than 30:1, but Toro adds that results vary by material, and a percentage claim is not measured the same way. Compare the Toro on airflow, build and warranty, not on that figure.

### Which ratio is enough?

For a yard where you bag leaves for curbside pickup, 16:1 or better keeps the bag count manageable. If you compost the mulch or spread it under shrubs, a lower ratio matters less because you are not paying for bags or hauling them to the curb.

sections.heading: How Big a Bag Does a Leaf Vacuum Need?
sections.body:
For a quarter-acre lot with a few trees, look for at least 1.2 bushels; below 1 bushel you will be walking to the bin constantly. A US bushel is about 9.3 gallons, so the 1.2-bushel WG509 bag holds roughly 11 gallons of mulch, and the 18-gallon Sun Joe bag holds close to 2 bushels.

### Bag size and ratio multiply

The two specs work together. An 11-gallon bag at 18:1 holds the equivalent of about 200 gallons of loose leaves on paper, roughly three and a half 55-gallon contractor bags. The WG583 bag, at 1.0 bushel and 12:1, holds about 110 gallons of loose leaves by the same math, a little more than half as much per trip. That gap is why the cordless WORX suits beds and patios better than a full lawn.

### The weight on your shoulder

A bigger bag also hangs heavier once it is full, because mulched leaves are dense. Emptying at two-thirds full spares your shoulder and keeps airflow up. If you have back or shoulder trouble, a wheeled design like the Ryobi or a push sweeper that rolls its load is worth the loss of reach.

### Collection kits

For big jobs, look for a kit that sends mulch straight into a yard-waste bag. WORX sells a leaf collection system bundle for its TriVac line, and the BV6600 manual lists a disposable-bag option. That turns emptying a shoulder bag into swapping a full paper bag for an empty one.

sections.heading: Corded or Cordless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher: Which Should You Buy?
sections.body:
Buy corded unless your leaves are far from an outlet or you already own batteries from one brand. Vacuuming and shredding take steady power, and a corded tool never quits halfway through a pile. The corded picks here draw 12 to 14 amps from a standard outlet.

### Living with the cord

You need an outdoor-rated extension cord of the gauge the manual specifies, plugged into a GFCI-protected outlet. Plan your route so you work away from the outlet with the slack trailing behind you, and keep the cord clear of the intake. A cord hook on your belt stops it from pulling the plug.

### What batteries change

Battery models trade runtime for freedom. Ryobi quotes more than 30 minutes from a 40V 4Ah pack on the RY40451, and the WORX WG583 runs on two 20V packs that fit the rest of the WORX range. Half an hour covers beds, a patio and a driveway edge; it does not cover a full autumn lot without a second battery on the charger.

Battery tools also post lower mulch ratios and smaller bags. The WG583 is rated 12:1 with a 1.0-bushel bag, against 18:1 and 1.2 bushels for its corded sibling. If you already own Ryobi 40V or WORX 20V tools, the bare-tool versions are cheap ways in. If you own neither, a corded model gives you more shredding for less money, and the same logic applies to trimmers in our [weed eater guide](/best-weed-eater/).

sections.heading: Can a Leaf Vacuum Pick Up Wet Leaves and Grass?
sections.body:
Not well. Wet leaves are the top cause of clogs, and makers generally tell you to vacuum dry material. Damp leaves cling to the tube walls, pack around the impeller and turn to paste in the bag, which chokes airflow and fills the bag with weight instead of volume. Fresh grass clippings behave the same way.

### How to avoid a jam

Work in the afternoon once the dew has burned off, or on a dry day after rain. Approach a pile from the edge at an angle instead of plunging the tube into the middle; one huge mouthful is what blocks the intake. Keep sticks, pine cones, stones and acorns out, because they nick the impeller and are the usual reason a tool rattles after one season.

### When suction drops

Check the bag before the impeller. A fabric bag caked with dust or wet residue stops breathing, so shake it out after each session and let it dry fully before storing it. If you rinse it, make sure it is bone dry before the next use.

### Clearing a clog

Stop, unplug the cord or pull the battery, and wait for the impeller to stop spinning. Then open the intake and clear the jam with gloves or a stick. For a soggy, matted layer on turf, skip the vacuum and mow it: a mulching mower chops wet leaves back into the lawn in a pass or two, and our [gas lawn mower picks](/best-gas-lawn-mowers/) include strong mulching decks.

sections.heading: Does a Metal Impeller Matter on a Leaf Vacuum?
sections.body:
Yes. The impeller takes the hit from every stick and acorn, so its material is the best single predictor of how long a leaf vacuum lasts. Five of the six powered picks state metal: WORX lists a two-stage metal impeller on the WG509, Toro metal impeller blades, Sun Joe an aluminum alloy impeller, BLACK+DECKER a high-impact metal fan, and Ryobi a metal impeller. WORX describes the WG583 impeller as two-stage without naming the material.

### Why plastic fails

The cheapest blower/vacs use plastic impellers. They chip on debris, and a chipped impeller vibrates, shreds poorly and eventually cracks. A damaged fan is a common reason an inexpensive blower/vac loses suction after a season or two, which is why no plastic-impeller model made this list.

### Metal still needs checking

A stone can bend a metal blade and throw it out of balance. Once a season, unplug the tool or remove the battery and look at the impeller for nicks, bends or wrapped string. If it buzzes or shakes, check whether the maker sells a replacement impeller before you replace the whole tool.

sections.heading: Is a Leaf Vacuum Better Than a Mower or Lawn Sweeper?
sections.body:
A leaf vacuum is the better tool when most of your leaves land in beds, along fences, on patios and in corners, or when your town wants leaves bagged at the curb. It is the wrong tool for an acre of open grass, where you would spend hours filling small bags.

### Match the tool to the yard

| Yard | Best approach |
| --- | --- |
| Under 1/4 acre with beds and hardscape | Corded 3-in-1 such as the WG509 or SBJ606E |
| 1/4 to 1/2 acre, mostly lawn | Blow onto tarps or into piles, then vacuum the piles |
| Over 1/2 acre of open lawn | Mulching mower or sweeper; vacuum only the beds |

### Where sweepers fit

Push sweepers like the Agri-Fab 45-0218 are the low-tech answer for lawns. Brushes geared to the wheels flick leaves into a hopper as you walk. The 6.2 cubic foot hopper holds about 46 gallons, roughly 5 bushels. Sweepers do not mulch, struggle when leaves are wet and cannot reach into beds, but they are quiet and need nothing but you.

On bigger properties, a riding mower or tractor with a bagger or tow-behind sweeper beats every handheld; see our [zero-turn mower guide](/best-zero-turn-mower/) and [compact tractor picks](/best-compact-tractor/) if you are already shopping for one.

sections.heading: How Do You Use a Leaf Vacuum Safely?
sections.body:
Wear safety glasses and hearing protection every time, and disconnect power and wait for the impeller to stop before you touch the tube, bag or impeller. Those two habits prevent most leaf vacuum injuries. Never vacuum ashes, liquids, glass or anything that could still be hot.

### Eyes, ears and lungs

In vacuum mode a stone or twig can kick back out of the intake, and blower mode throws grit everywhere, so eye protection is not optional. Blower/vacs are loud at arm's length, and foam plugs or earmuffs are cheap insurance. Shredding dry leaves raises dust and mold spores; a simple dust mask helps anyone with allergies or asthma.

### Cords, guards and clothing

Plug corded tools into a GFCI-protected outdoor outlet and keep the cord behind you. Never run a vacuum with the bag unzipped or removed; Toro's manual warns against both, and the UltraPlus will not run unless the vacuum tube is locked in place. Keep loose sleeves, drawstrings and long hair away from the intake, and wear closed shoes and long pants.

### Around people and pets

Keep children and pets back while you work, since the blower can throw debris well past the tool. Point the blower away from cars, windows and neighbors, and save the noisiest work for reasonable hours.

mistakes.title: Vacuuming wet leaves
mistakes.body: Damp leaves smear onto the tube, pack the impeller and turn the bag into a heavy, airless sack. Wait for a dry afternoon, or mow a soggy layer back into the lawn instead of fighting a clogged intake.

mistakes.title: Buying on blower MPH
mistakes.body: Top blowing speed is the headline on most boxes, but it says little about vacuuming. For a leaf vacuum, mulch ratio, bag capacity and impeller material decide how fast the job goes. Compare those first.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the impeller material
mistakes.body: A plastic impeller chips on the first acorn or twig and loses suction within a season or two. Choose a model that states a metal impeller or fan, and inspect it each fall for nicks and wrapped debris.

mistakes.title: Trying to vacuum a whole lawn
mistakes.body: A handheld intake is a few inches wide and the bag holds about a bushel. On open turf, blow leaves into piles or use a sweeper or mulching mower, and save the vacuum for beds, corners and hardscape.

mistakes.title: Reaching in with the power on
mistakes.body: Clearing a jam with the cord plugged in or the battery attached is how fingers meet a spinning impeller. Disconnect power, wait for the impeller to stop completely, and use gloves or a stick to clear the blockage.

faqs.q: What is the best leaf vacuum mulcher?
faqs.a: The WORX WG509 TriVac is the best leaf vacuum mulcher for most yards. WORX rates it at 18:1 through a two-stage metal impeller and shredder blade, feeding a 1.2-bushel bag, and it carries a 3-year warranty. If you want a larger bag, the Sun Joe SBJ606E holds 18 gallons at 16:1. For cordless shredding, the Ryobi 40V RY40451 is rated 16:1.

faqs.q: What is the best cordless leaf vacuum shredder?
faqs.a: The Ryobi 40V RY40451 is the best cordless leaf vacuum shredder here because Ryobi rates it at 16:1 through a metal impeller, with over 30 minutes of runtime on a 4Ah battery. It has no blower mode. If you want a cordless 3-in-1 that blows too, the WORX WG583 weighs 8.4 pounds with batteries but mulches at 12:1.

faqs.q: What is the best lightweight cordless blower vacuum and mulcher?
faqs.a: The WORX WG583 40V is the lightest powered pick, at 5.5 pounds bare and 8.4 pounds with its two 20V batteries installed. WORX lists 350 CFM, a 12:1 mulch ratio and a 1.0-bushel bag. It is best for beds, patios and small yards; a full suburban lot will need spare batteries or a corded tool.

faqs.q: Is a leaf blower/vacuum worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if most of your leaves land in beds, corners, along fences or on hardscape, or if your town requires bagged leaves. A 16:1 mulcher turns sixteen bags of loose leaves into roughly one. It is not worth it for open lawns over half an acre, where a mulching mower or push sweeper clears leaves much faster.

faqs.q: Can a leaf vacuum pick up grass clippings?
faqs.a: Only dry ones, and only in small amounts. Fresh, damp clippings pack the tube and impeller the same way wet leaves do. Makers generally recommend vacuuming dry material. For clippings on a lawn, a mower with a bag or mulching deck is the better tool, and the vacuum is best kept for dry leaves and debris on hard surfaces.

faqs.q: What does a 16:1 mulch ratio mean?
faqs.a: It means sixteen bags of loose, dry leaves should shrink to one bag after shredding, by the maker's own rating. Real results fall short when leaves are damp or mixed with twigs. Use the ratio to compare tools: an 18:1 vacuum fills about 11% fewer bags than a 16:1, and a 12:1 fills about a third more.

faqs.q: Which leaf vacuum has the biggest suction bag?
faqs.a: Among the handhelds here, the Sun Joe SBJ606E has the biggest bag at 18 gallons, close to 2 bushels, paired with a 14-amp motor and 440 CFM of rated vacuum airflow. The Agri-Fab 45-0218 push sweeper holds far more, 6.2 cubic feet or about 46 gallons, but it does not vacuum or mulch.

bottomLine: For most yards, the WORX WG509 TriVac is the leaf vacuum to buy: an 18:1 rated mulch ratio, a metal impeller, a 1.2-bushel bag and a 3-year warranty in a 9.3-pound corded tool. Step to the Toro UltraPlus 51621 if you want the most suction, the Sun Joe SBJ606E if bag size matters most, or the Ryobi RY40451 if you want cordless shredding at 16:1. Vacuum dry leaves only, empty the bag before it gets heavy, check the impeller every fall, and hand open lawns to a sweeper or mulching mower.
